Main evidence: Visual-supported targets accounted for the observed Recall@20 and NDCG@20 gains; image-less targets remained outside the top 20 under both models.
Interpretation: Visual availability is associated with where multimodal benefit can occur, but is confounded with interaction support and metadata richness.

Main evidence: Adjusted top-K coefficients were positive but 95% cluster-robust confidence intervals included zero for NDCG@10, Recall@20 and NDCG@20.
Interpretation: More available photographs alone did not clearly identify businesses receiving stronger top-K multimodal benefit.

Main evidence: Adjusted associations were positive for NDCG@10, Recall@20 and NDCG@20, with all 95% confidence intervals above zero.
Interpretation: Greater diversity in visual evidence was consistently associated with stronger multimodal recommendation gains.

Main evidence: Low-support businesses showed large positive rank movement but remained far outside the top 20; only high-support businesses showed non-zero top-K effects.
Interpretation: Visual information can substantially improve relative rank for sparse businesses, but sufficient baseline support is needed for those gains to translate into top-K exposure.

Main evidence: Sparse-history users showed positive Recall@20 and NDCG@20 effects, with sparse-minus-dense contrasts whose bootstrap confidence intervals excluded zero.
Interpretation: Multimodal evidence appears particularly useful for top-20 recommendation effectiveness when user preference history is limited.

Main evidence: Removing target visual information strongly reduced target scores/ranks for visual-supported businesses, while catalogue-wide visual masking reduced top-K effectiveness.
Interpretation: The trained multimodal model actively relies on its visual pathway, but these perturbations measure model sensitivity rather than causal visual contribution.
